summary.summary: Wakefield's 2025/26 treasury outturn was fully compliant: the CFR rose £13.5m to £571.3m while external borrowing actually fell £3.1m to £377.9m (PWLB £346.4m, other local authorities £26.5m, banks £5m), leaving the council £131.9m under-borrowed and running on internal cash — capital slippage saved £4.2m of borrowing costs and the treasury budget underspent £3.85m. The average rate paid on external debt was 4.80%, and the council flags that the LA-to-LA borrowing market is 'becoming tight' as other authorities chase the same borrow-short-until-rates-fall strategy; investments stood at £57m (£40m in the DMO deposit facility, £17m lent to other councils). A legacy MRP overpayment that has been suppressing the revenue charge for debt is nearly exhausted — £5.3m left, fully used by end-2026/27, after which all MRP hits the revenue budget. Financing costs ran at 11.30% of net revenue (9.68% excluding PFI) against budgets of 13.16% and 9.70%.
summary.as_of_doc: Treasury Management for the year ending 31 March 2026.

signals.headline: £131.9m under-borrowed against the £571.3m CFR at 31 March 2026, on a deliberate short-term debt stance, while the council itself reports the LA-to-LA borrowing market 'becoming tight'
signals.why: The deferred borrowing need must eventually be financed externally, and the council's preferred market for short money is the one it says is tightening.

signals.headline: Legacy MRP overpayment offset down to £5.3m at 31 March 2026 and fully utilised by end-2026/27 — thereafter all MRP is charged to the revenue budget; the average rate paid on external borrowing was already 4.80% in 2025/26
signals.why: A structural step-up in the revenue cost of debt arrives from 2027/28, just as deferred borrowing may need to be externalised at current rates.

compliance.notes: Strong, professionally advised (Link) combined capital + treasury strategy: prudential indicators, a 10-year liability benchmark, MRP policy, borrowing strategy and creditworthiness/counterparty policy are all well developed, and every applicable core requirement scores >=2. Weakest areas are the non-treasury/commercial-investment framework (no explicit paras 51-53 compliance statement, no confirmed IMPs, no monetary limits on service/commercial investment, thin statutory disclosures, guarantees not reassessed), the absence of a quantitative investment-portfolio risk indicator (INV-06), accounts-linked reporting items not evidenced in the strategy (audit-qualification flag, financial-instruments disclosures), and ESG which is only referenced as a future Code requirement. Note: the documents contain no HRA content (housing stock transferred to WDH), so HRA-split and separate-HRA-benchmark elements are treated as not applicable.

news_drafts.headline: Wakefield forecasts £10.3m schools-grant deficit at March 2027, with government override extended to 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Wakefield Council forecasts a deficit of £10.3m on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) at the end of 2026/27, according to the medium-term financial strategy (the council's financial plan for the next three to five years) put to Cabinet on 20 October 2026.

The high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, is forecast to overspend by £9.9m in 2026/27. The paper calls it "the driver for the overspend". It says that overspend increases the overall forecast deficit on the grant to £10.3m at the end of the financial year.

The deficit currently sits outside the council's main budget under a statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet. The paper says the arrangement "was previously due to end in March 2026; however, Government have extended this until March 2028". It states that when the override ends, the deficit will revert to the main budget unless the underlying pressures on special educational needs and disabilities spending are resolved.

news_drafts.headline: Wakefield cuts capital programme by £56m as spending lags and oversight remains incomplete
news_drafts.lead: Wakefield Council has reduced its five-year capital programme from £414.7m to £358.5m in the first quarter of 2026-27, with a further reprofiling planned within weeks. Capital spending in the first three months reached only £22m against a projected £138m quarterly rate, running at 15.9 per cent of profile. The revised programme relies on £140.2m of prudential borrowing (borrowing to fund long-lived assets), representing 39 per cent of total spending, but the council has provided no detailed assessment of how this will affect the revenue budget. The Cabinet papers acknowledge that governance arrangements for the capital programme are currently under review and do not yet fully embed the Duty of Best Value. A further reprofile and budget challenge will take place in the second quarter.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Report - Q2 2627 For Cabinet
findings.headline: Future capital business cases will be reviewed by an Officer Review Group, which was set up to support the S151 officer.
findings.detail: The paper says the Officer Review Group assesses whether budgets are robust and deliverable. It also says governance arrangements for the capital programme remain under review.
findings.matters: A new review step on business cases before approval is a change to capital governance that other S151 officers may be weighing for their own programmes.
findings.quote: which was established to support the S151 officer to assess whether budgets are both robust and deliverable.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Report - Q2 2627 For Cabinet
findings.headline: Wakefield has bought Unit K, Kenmore Road, Wakefield 41 Industrial Park, at a cost of £6.8m including SDLT and VAT, acting as lead authority for YPO.
findings.detail: YPO is not a separate legal entity, so Wakefield holds the freehold on trust for YPO under the management agreement with the member authorities. The Prostar building was bought for warehousing, and the paper says the budget is funded in full from YPO, which will transfer the funds to the Council.
findings.matters: Councils that hold assets on behalf of joint bodies can see how a lead authority carries property and funding for a joint arrangement.
findings.figures: £6.8m acquisition cost including SDLT and VAT (reclaimable); funded in full from YPO resources
findings.quote: The cost of the acquisition is £6.8m including Stamp Duty & Land Tax (SDLT), and VAT, which can be reclaimed by the Council.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Report - Q2 2627 For Cabinet
findings.headline: The MRP charge for 2026/27, based on expenditure up to 31 March 2026, is expected to be £11.2m.
findings.detail: The paper links the MRP charge to the prudential-borrowing profile and gives an illustration: £1m of annual revenue funding per £10m of borrowing at an assumed 6.5% rate over 25 years.
findings.matters: MRP is a fixed revenue cost that follows past capital spend, so finance directors compare it against the revenue budget when judging affordability.
findings.figures: £11.2m expected 2026/27 MRP charge; £1m annual revenue cost per £10m of prudential borrowing (illustrative, 6.5% rate, 25-year life)

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Report - Q2 2627 For Cabinet
findings.headline: The revised capital programme for 2026/27 to 2030/31 totals £381.6m, underpinned by £140.2m of prudential borrowing.
findings.detail: The paper says the programme covers approved schemes up to 31 August 2026 and excludes pipeline schemes still in development. It also says every prudential-borrowing project carries revenue costs through MRP and borrowing costs.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the scale of prudential borrowing relative to the total programme and the revenue cost it implies.
findings.figures: £381.6m total programme (£381,634k); £140.2m prudential borrowing (£140,168k); £160.2m government grants (£160,238k)
findings.quote: underpinned by £140.2m of prudential borrowing with the delivery profile

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Report - Q2 2627 For Cabinet
findings.headline: The Q2 2026/27 capital budget is £114.5m, against £130.3m approved by Council in March 2026, a reduction of £15.8m.
findings.detail: Table 2 shows the Q1 budget at £138.1m and Q2 at £114.5m. Against the March approval, Regeneration, Environment and Economic Growth is down £11.2m and Schools is down £7.2m, while Resources is up £1.2m.
findings.matters: A council's budget falling this far from what was approved in March, across two directorates in one quarter, is a movement a peer or lender would want to see explained.
findings.figures: £114,538k Q2 budget; £130,334k approved budget (2 March 2026); £138,053k Q1 budget; (£15,796k) Q2 variance to approved; (£11,223k) Regeneration variance; (£7,209k) Schools variance; £1,243k Resources variance

daily_post.headline: Cabinet is asked to agree that all new and existing fees be set at full cost recovery, market sensitive, reviewed at least annually and adjusted for cost increases.
daily_post.lead: A policy requiring full cost recovery on all fees is a specific income lever that other councils facing similar gaps may consider adopting.
